models.summary: 12 indices in three dimensions, School Development, Student Treatment, Social Influence, drawn from 20 data sets for 22 countries. Benefit, cost, and moderate indices normalized separately; moderate indices reward closeness to a stated target such as 5 percent of spending or a 10:4:1 degree mix. Weights blend group decision making at 0.85 with entropy weights at 0.15. The three scores form a vector S. Its modulus measures health, its angle to (1,1,1) measures imbalance, by the Cannikin argument. UK angle 1.15 degrees, US modulus 1.278, India modulus 0.735 and angle 23.13 degrees.
models.purpose: Score a national higher education system on both level and balance, so the weak country can be chosen for policy work.
objectives: Separate the health of the system from the balance of its three parts, and keep both visible.

details: 22 countries on all continents, 20 data sets collapsed to 12 indices. Sources: UNESCO, World Bank, national databases.
Moderate targets: spending share near 5 percent, degree mix near 10:4:1, gender ratio near 1:1, exchange and admission shares near 3 percent.
Index model. The standard vector (1,1,1) is an ideal, not an equilibrium.

parameter_estimation.method: Expert matrices averaged with equal weights, checked for consistency, then blended with entropy weights at 0.85 and 0.15.

algorithm.description: Classify indices, fill gaps three ways, normalize by type, blend two weight methods, form the vector, read modulus and angle.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: All three judgment matrices pass the consistency check.

details: Eight countries scored. UK angle 1.15 degrees, US modulus 1.278, India 0.735 and 23.13 degrees, South Africa angle 30.65 degrees. India components SD 0.46, ST 0.54, SI 0.16.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The two readings separate the countries: the US leads on length, the UK on balance. That split is the reason India, weak on both, is the case.

strengths: Modulus and angle keep level and balance from collapsing into one rank.
The moderate-type rule stops a rich country from scoring by overspending.
limitations: The 0.85 and 0.15 blend is stated, not derived.
Expert scores are not shown, only the resulting vectors.
GDM vectors have four entries while the printed index table is hard to align with them.
missing_details: Number of experts and their matrices.
Which index occupies which slot in the four-entry weight vectors.
assumptions: A student's system is fixed by nationality.
Experts are equally skilled and the questions are unambiguous.
Development is continuous and slow, with no mutation.

models.summary: The ideal (1,1,1) is declared unreachable in one step. Two elasticity indicators built from HDI, the Fragile States Index, and the Gini coefficient move the target: Em stretches the modulus, E-theta shrinks the allowed angle. For India the target is a spherical cap of radius 1.22 inside an 11.5 degree cone. The cheap edge point exploits India's stronger SD and ST. Reaching it means gains of 41.3, 20.4, and 306 percent on the three components.
models.purpose: Turn the ideal vector into a target a named country could actually reach, and keep the target a region rather than a point.
objectives: Set a feasible health level and a balance range that respect non-educational limits.

algorithm.description: Score three non-educational indices, compute two elasticities, push the radius toward sqrt(3), shrink the angle, draw the cap.

details: India: radius 1.22, cone 11.5 degrees. Edge point gains 41.3, 20.4, and 306 percent.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The 306 percent gain on social influence is the whole policy story, and it rests on coefficients nobody estimated.

constraints: Path expected to curve, since pushing one component disturbs the others.
strengths: A region target is more honest than a point target.
The missing-variable objection is answered by showing GDP per capita already sits inside HDI and FSI.
limitations: Coefficients are round numbers with no source.
Text and sensitivity table disagree on two coefficients by a factor of 100.
missing_details: India's actual HDI, FSI, and Gini values.
How the edge point OP was chosen numerically.
assumptions: Non-educational factors cap the education target.
Balance is the first task regardless of how strong the system becomes.
No mutation, so the path is slow.

models.summary: Short series rule out ordinary forecasting, so an improved grey Verhulst model predicts the three components with no policy. The series is inverted, accumulated, and fit. Without policy, student treatment falls 3.2 percent a year and the summary sheet puts the system at modulus 0.640 and angle 29.96 degrees. With policy, student treatment rises 0.6 percent, social influence growth goes from 3.1 to 5.8 percent, and school development stays at 1.1 percent. The 2040 vector is (0.58, 0.61, 0.50), modulus about 0.98, angle under 11.5 degrees. The summary sheet states 0.978 and 4.86 degrees.
models.purpose: Show the policy changes the direction of student treatment and the speed of social influence.
objectives: Forecast each component over 20 years twice, once untouched and once under the stated policy.

details: Recent annual rates: ST falls 3.2 percent, SI grows 3.1 percent, SD grows 1.1 percent.
Forecast horizon 20 years, to 2040. Saturation is expected, which is why Verhulst is chosen.
The Verhulst form has a saturation level, but the paper never states its value.

parameter_estimation.method: Grey parameters (a, b, c) are estimated from the short reciprocal series. The estimation formula is not legible.

algorithm.description: Invert each component series, accumulate, fit the three-parameter grey equation, invert back, compare the no-policy path with the policy path.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Not stated. No error table is given.

details: 2040 vector (0.58, 0.61, 0.50). Summary sheet: no policy modulus 0.640 and angle 29.96 degrees; with policy 0.978 and 4.86 degrees.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The direction change in student treatment, from minus 3.2 to plus 0.6 percent, is the result that carries the policy. No fit error is reported.

constraints: No mutation, so the grey smoothness assumption holds.
strengths: The no-policy path is shown first, so the policy has something to beat.
Choosing a saturating model matches the assumption that the system cannot grow without limit.
limitations: No residual, no MAPE, no hold-out year.
The policy path is asserted rather than generated by the same equation.
missing_details: How the policy changes the series inside the model.
assumptions: The short series is enough for a grey model.
The policy changes rates but not the model form.
